topics.title: Classes, properties and individuals
topics.what_it_is: A class is a set of things that share a kind, such as Lecture or Person. An individual is one named thing, such as the lecture CNN4. An object property links two individuals; a data property links an individual to a literal value. A class assertion says an individual belongs to a class; a property assertion says two things are linked. In OWL 2 the same IRI can be used as a class and as an individual (punning); reasoners treat the two uses as different. Classes and properties form the vocabulary; individuals and their assertions form the data.
topics.why: Entity extraction in GraphRAG has to decide: is 'Backpropagation' a class (a kind of thing), an individual (one named topic) or both? Mixing them breaks type-aware retrieval. A clear split gives clean 'rdf:type' triples and makes the class list usable as an extraction prompt.

formulas.latex: a^{\mathcal I}\in\Delta^{\mathcal I},\qquad C^{\mathcal I}\subseteq\Delta^{\mathcal I},\qquad R^{\mathcal I}\subseteq\Delta^{\mathcal I}\times\Delta^{\mathcal I};\qquad C(a)\text{ holds iff }a^{\mathcal I}\in C^{\mathcal I},\quad R(a,b)\text{ holds iff }(a^{\mathcal I},b^{\mathcal I})\in R^{\mathcal I}
formulas.name: Semantic reading of the three kinds of entity

steps: Decide for each term: kind of thing (class), one thing (individual), link (property), value link (data property).
Declare them with a standard vocabulary (owl:Class, owl:ObjectProperty, owl:DatatypeProperty).
Give each property a domain and range.
Write assertions: 'ex:l1 a ex:Lecture' and 'ex:l1 ex:covers ex:Backprop'.
Check with a reasoner for unsatisfiable classes.
trade_offs: Punning lets one IRI be a class and an individual. It is legal in OWL 2 DL but confuses people and some tools.
A class is not an instance of its superclass: CNN subClassOf NeuralNetwork does not make CNN a NeuralNetwork.
Datatype properties take literals; object properties take IRIs. Mixing them makes the ontology outside OWL 2 DL.
Over-modelling kinds as classes yields thousands of classes with one instance each.

topics.title: Ontologies and knowledge graphs for CS, ML and AI
topics.what_it_is: The Computer Science Ontology (CSO, 2018) is a large taxonomy of research areas. Its authors say that the ACM classification has only about 2K topics and its last version dates back to 2012. AI-KG (2020) and CS-KG (2022, 2.0 in 2025) are knowledge graphs of research entities extracted from papers. ML-Schema (2018) is a top-level ontology for machine-learning algorithms, datasets and experiments. The Artificial Intelligence Ontology (AIO, 2024) systematises AI concepts, built by manual curation with LLM help.
topics.why: These are ready vocabularies for a CS or ML course graph: alignment targets for concept ids, and schema examples. They model research literature, not teaching, so they have no prerequisite relation. Use them for names and links, not as the whole schema.

inputs: Course concepts or extracted entity names
outputs: Alignment ids (CSO topic, AIO term, ML-Schema class) per concept

steps: Pick the target ontologies by licence and freshness.
Normalise concept names (case, plural, hyphens).
Match names and synonyms to ontology labels.
Review unmatched concepts by hand or with an LLM proposal.
Store the alignment ids as properties of the graph nodes.
trade_offs: Coverage is low for narrow course concepts: only 21 of 662 nodes matched AIO exactly in the real test below.
Ontologies age at different speeds: AIO had a release dated 2026-07-22; CSO v3.5 is dated 29 Jul 2025 on its page; ML-Schema and ITO repositories are stale per the vault note.
Licences differ (the vault note lists CC BY 4.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 AT for ITO); check before redistributing.

worked_example.description: Cheap re-verification plus a real matching test. AIO release 2026-07-22 (data-version line of aio.obo) has 442 [Term] entries, as in the vault note; with synonyms it has 873 distinct names. We matched the 662 node names of the real graph against those names (lowercase, punctuation removed, simple plural handling): 21 nodes match, 17 of them typed Method (of 224 Method nodes, 7.6%), for example decision tree, linear regression, random forests, SVM, principal component analysis, perceptron. CSO page: "about 15K topics linked by 166K semantic relationships", release 29 Jul 2025.
worked_example.note: Exact-name matching only: it undercounts (no stemming beyond plural, no embedding match). The synonym count is our parse of the synonym lines. CSO was not matched (large file).

topics.title: Education ontologies: learning-object metadata, Bloom, prerequisites, curriculum
topics.what_it_is: Education has its own vocabularies. IEEE 1484.12.1 is a standard for learning object metadata (LOM). Bloom's taxonomy (1956) classifies educational goals, and Krathwohl (2002) gives an overview of its revision. Prerequisite-relation learning finds which concept must be learned before another. Liang et al. (2015) propose a link-based metric, reference distance (RefD), and Pan et al. (2017) learn prerequisites in MOOCs. Christou et al. (2025) present a Curriculum KG Ontology that links educational materials.
topics.why: A tutoring GraphRAG needs more than topic links: it needs prerequisite edges, learning-goal levels and material metadata. Stancin et al. (2020) review ontologies in education. Existing CS ontologies (see the next topic) hold research topics, not prerequisites, so the education layer has to be added.

inputs: Wikipedia links or text for prerequisite scoring

symbols.c_i: the i-th concept of the concept space C (k concepts)
symbols.r(c_i, B): 1 if c_i refers to B (for example links to the Wikipedia article B), else 0
symbols.w(c_i, A): importance of c_i to A; EQUAL weighting: 1 if c_i is linked from A, else 0
symbols.RefD(A,B): value in [-1, 1]; above a threshold theta, A requires B as prerequisite; theta between 0.02 and 0.1 worked well in the paper

steps: Pick the concept set from a course or from Wikipedia.
Score concept pairs: RefD from links, or a model trained on labelled pairs (Pan et al. 2017).
Keep pairs above a threshold as prerequisite-of edges.
Add metadata for each learning object (LOM fields) and a goal level (Bloom) per outcome.
Have a teacher review the edges.
trade_offs: RefD depends on Wikipedia articles: concepts without or with short articles score poorly (the paper names "discriminative model" and "feature engineering").
Prerequisite labels are subjective: datasets differ between domains and annotators.
LOM and Bloom descriptions here are title-level: the standard and the 2002 paper are paywalled and were not read.

worked_example.description: Verified example from the RefD paper (Table 4, EQUAL weighting): RefD("deep learning", c) for concepts linked from the "deep learning" article. Negative values mean deep learning is a prerequisite of c: Deep belief network -0.38, Neocognitron -0.28, Word embedding -0.24. Positive values mean deep learning requires c: Machine learning 0.32, Artificial neural network 0.31, Artificial intelligence 0.15, Algorithm 0.14. Values near zero mean no prerequisite relation (List of Nobel laureates 0.009). Our own real data: the LLM extraction of the ML-article pack has 28 "requires" edges (for example linear regression models requires multicollinearity, lasso requires sparse coefficients); none has been checked against a prerequisite gold set.
worked_example.computed_by: Table 4 values copied from the paper PDF (page 5, 2015 EMNLP); requires count read from stats.json
worked_example.note: We did not recompute RefD: it needs Wikipedia link data for the whole concept space.

topics.title: Checking graph quality with an ontology
topics.what_it_is: An ontology gives rules to test a knowledge graph. Domain and range say which types a relation may link. Disjoint classes say what cannot overlap. Zaveri et al. (2015) and Paulheim (2016) survey quality assessment and error detection for Linked Data and knowledge graphs. Serles and Fensel (2024, chapter 20) list 14 quality dimensions, including accuracy and completeness. Text2KGBench adds a conformance metric for LLM-built graphs.
topics.why: LLM extraction is the main source of errors in a GraphRAG index. A report of constraint violations is a cheap early warning: you fix the prompt or the schema before you debug retrieval.

inputs: Ontology rules: allowed relations, domain and range, disjointness, cardinality

symbols.T_conf: output triples whose relation is in the ontology

steps: List the rules from the ontology.
Run each rule over the graph.
Count violations per rule.
Review a sample by hand: decide whether the triple or the rule is wrong.
Feed back: change the prompt, the schema or the merge rules.
trade_offs: A passing graph is not a true graph: rules test form, not facts.
Rules written after seeing the data can hide real problems; write them before.
Quality dimensions can conflict: strict rules may lower completeness (our reading, not a cited result).

worked_example.description: Four checks on the real graph, by code. (1) Label conformance of raw output: 742 of 781 relations use a listed label (95.0%). (2) Type conformance of raw entities: 895 of 905 (98.9%). (3) Dangling endpoints: 24 of 781 raw relations name an entity that is not in the answer's entity list. (4) Range of introduced_by (Person or Organization): 28 of 43 pass, 12 are reversed, 3 have another type. In addition, 29 of 87 subclass edges link nodes of different types.
worked_example.computed_by: python over raw files and graph.json
worked_example.note: Rules (3) and (4) are ours, written for this illustration.

topics.title: Populating an ontology with an LLM and validating the result with SHACL
topics.what_it_is: Ontology population fills the ontology with instances (the A-box) taken from text. When an LLM does it, the output must be checked against the schema. SHACL, a W3C Recommendation from 2017, is a language for validating RDF graphs against a set of conditions called shapes. Text2KGBench measures this with an ontology-conformance metric: the share of LLM output triples that conform to the input ontology. In that version, conforming means the relation is in the ontology; the authors say it can be extended to domain and range.
topics.why: LLM extraction makes mistakes that look fluent. A validation layer rejects triples whose relation, domain or range break the schema before they reach the retriever. It also gives a number (conformance) to track from run to run.

inputs: A schema: allowed relations, domain and range (as SHACL shapes in an RDF stack)
outputs: A violation report (which triple broke which constraint)

symbols.T_out: all triples in the LLM output
symbols.T_conf: triples in T_out whose relation is one of the canonical relations of the input ontology

steps: Define shapes: which relations are allowed, with which subject and object types.
Run the LLM extraction.
Convert the output to RDF triples.
Validate against the shapes; collect the report.
Repair or reject violating triples; log the conformance rate.
trade_offs: A shape can reject a true triple whose type was mislabelled: the check judges form, not truth.
The OC definition of Text2KGBench only checks the relation label, so a conforming triple can still have a wrong subject type.
SHACL assumes an RDF stack; a property-graph store needs equivalent checks written as queries or constraints.

worked_example.description: OC computed on the real raw output with the Text2KGBench definition (relation label in the allowed list of 13): (781 - 39) / 781 = 0.950. A domain/range-style check that we wrote ourselves for introduced_by (range must be Person or Organization) flags 15 of the 43 final edges: 12 point the wrong way (a Person is the source, for example Koltchinskii introduced_by oracle inequalities) and 3 have another type.
worked_example.note: The introduced_by signature (range Person or Organization) is our own rule for illustration, not a published shape. The lasso -> geophysics edge is textually defensible (the passage says lasso was first used in geophysics) yet violates the rule: validation finds candidates for review.

topics.title: Schema-guided knowledge-graph extraction with LLMs
topics.what_it_is: Schema-guided extraction asks an LLM to read text and return facts that follow a given schema or ontology. Text2KGBench (2023) defines the task. Given an ontology and sentences, extract facts that follow its concepts, relations and domain/range constraints and match the text. Extract-Define-Canonicalize (2024) notes that prior methods put the whole schema into the prompt. That stops working when the schema is large or complex.
topics.why: The extraction prompt decides what the graph can contain. A closed list of types and relations gives a clean graph that queries can use. It costs prompt tokens on every call and loses facts that do not fit the list.

inputs: Ontology or lists of entity types and relation labels
outputs: Triples (source, relation, target) with typed entities, as JSON

steps: Put the schema (types, relation labels, optional domain/range) and the rules into the prompt.
Give one passage, ask for JSON only.
Parse the JSON; drop or flag triples with labels outside the schema.
Merge duplicates (aliases) into nodes.
Measure conformance and fact accuracy against the schema and the text.
trade_offs: Closed lists force wrong labels: the real run shows the model invented labels outside the list for 39 of 781 relations.
Large schemas do not fit in a prompt (Zhang and Soh 2024, abstract); EDC extracts openly first, then defines and canonicalises labels.
Without gold facts you can measure conformance but not correctness.

worked_example.description: The real extraction prompt lists 9 entity types and 13 relation labels. We re-read the 138 raw model answers and counted how often the model followed the list: 781 raw relations, 39 used a label outside the 13 (5.0%); 905 raw entities, 10 had a type outside the 9 (all "Task"); 24 relations (3.1%) named an endpoint that was not in the same answer's entity list.
worked_example.source: Presentations/_real-examples/raw/graph/extract_p*.json (138 files, all parsed); prompt text in graph README section Extraction
worked_example.computed_by: python over raw/graph files (a local script; rerun reads the same cached files)
worked_example.note: Outside labels seen: has_property (8), controls (4), used_in (3), defines (3), prevents (2) and others. The pack then builds the graph with its own rules; this count is of the raw model output.

topics.title: Neo4j and the neosemantics (n10s) plugin
topics.what_it_is: Neo4j is a property graph database; neosemantics (n10s) is a Neo4j Labs plugin that adds RDF support. n10s imports and exports RDF (Turtle, N-Triples, JSON-LD, RDF/XML, TriG, N-Quads) and maps it to nodes, relationships and properties. It can import RDFS or OWL ontologies as class and property nodes with subclass (SCO) and subproperty (SPO) relationships. It validates a Neo4j graph against SHACL shapes (n10s.validation.shacl.*). It offers basic inferencing: query by a class or category together with its subcategories. It is not an OWL reasoner, and it is not available on Neo4j Aura (self-hosted only).
topics.why: Many GraphRAG stacks already use Neo4j. n10s lets them load an ontology or a SKOS vocabulary, keep IRIs, validate extracted triples with SHACL and expand a query to subclasses, all inside the graph database that holds the knowledge graph.

inputs: RDF data or an ontology file (URL or inline)
outputs: Neo4j nodes and relationships with uri properties

steps: Install the n10s plugin on a self-hosted Neo4j.
Create the uniqueness constraint on Resource.uri (as the docs state).
Run n10s.graphconfig.init (defaults: SHORTEN, OVERWRITE, LABELS) or pass a map.
Import RDF with n10s.rdf.import.fetch or an ontology with n10s.onto.import.fetch.
Load SHACL shapes with n10s.validation.shacl.import.fetch and run n10s.validation.shacl.validate().
Query categories with n10s.inference.nodesLabelled or nodesInCategory.
trade_offs: The Graph Config is global and cannot be changed after data is imported, until the graph is emptied (docs).
n10s imports only part of an OWL ontology: classes, subclass, properties, subproperty, domain and range. Everything else is ignored.
n10s covers a large part of SHACL but not all of it (docs).
n10s inference is hierarchy traversal, not OWL 2 DL reasoning.
The constraint syntax shown in the docs source is the older 'ON ... ASSERT' form; newer Neo4j versions use a different form (not verified here).

topics.title: OntoClean: checking a taxonomy with meta-properties
topics.what_it_is: OntoClean is a method by Guarino and Welty to check the is-a hierarchy of an ontology. It tags each class with meta-properties from philosophy: rigidity, identity, unity and dependence. A rule set then says which subclass links are wrong, for example a rigid class cannot be a subclass of an anti-rigid class. The aim is to find bad subsumption before it spreads to the data. The method is a manual analysis; tools support it but do not replace the judgement.
topics.why: LLM extraction produces many is-a edges. Some are not real subclass links but role, part or type-of-artefact confusions. OntoClean-style questions give a cheap review for those edges, before the retriever expands queries along them.

inputs: Analyst tags for each class: rigid or not, carries identity or not
outputs: A list of subsumption links that violate the meta-property constraints

steps: Tag each class with its meta-properties.
Check every subclass link against the constraints.
Mark violations.
Repair by changing the link, splitting the class, or turning a class into a role.
trade_offs: Manual and costly: it needs one expert judgement per class.
The meta-property definitions are subtle; wrong tags give wrong results.
It applies to a taxonomy of types, not to a graph of mixed relations.
Specific rule statements here come from the OntoClean papers by title and secondary knowledge; the full texts were not open access and were not read (see notes).

worked_example.description: An OntoClean-style review applied to the real graph, as an illustration. Of 87 subclass edges (is_a and special_case_of), 29 link nodes of different entity types (for example Method under Concept, Metric under Concept). One of them links a Method node to a Software node.
worked_example.note: This is an OntoClean-flavoured check, not a full OntoClean analysis: we did not tag rigidity or identity. A type-crossing edge is a candidate for review, not a proven error.

topics.title: What an ontology is: Gruber, Studer and Guarino
topics.what_it_is: Gruber (1993) calls a specification of a representational vocabulary for a shared domain of discourse an ontology. The vocabulary holds definitions of classes, relations, functions and other objects. Studer, Benjamins and Fensel (1998) merge two earlier definitions: an ontology is a formal, explicit specification of a shared conceptualisation. A conceptualisation is an abstract model of some phenomenon, made from its relevant concepts. Guarino (1995) argues that knowledge engineering needs formal ontological principles, not only ad-hoc vocabularies.
topics.why: A GraphRAG schema (entity types and relation labels in the extraction prompt) is a small ontology in this sense. The extractor and the retriever both commit to the same shared vocabulary. The definition also separates the vocabulary from the data: the graph holds the instances.

inputs: A domain and a community that must share terms
outputs: A vocabulary of classes and relations, written in an explicit (often formal) language

steps: Choose the domain and the shared purpose.
List the concepts that matter in the domain (the conceptualisation).
Write each class and relation down explicitly, with a definition.
Choose a formal language when machines must check or reason over it (OWL, SHACL).
Apply the vocabulary to data: instances form the knowledge graph.
trade_offs: Definitions differ: Gruber says vocabulary, Studer adds "formal" and "shared", Guarino stresses philosophical rigour (verified from Studer 1998 p. text; Guarino 1995 abstract).
A list of labels in a prompt is explicit but not formal: it has no axioms, so no reasoner can check it.
"Shared" is a social property, not a technical one: nobody can prove it from the file.

worked_example.description: The real-example pack fixes a closed vocabulary in its extraction prompt: 9 entity types and 13 relation labels. That vocabulary is a small ontology in the sense of Gruber and Studer: an explicit list of the classes and relations that 138 extraction calls had to commit to.

topics.title: Competency questions: the test an ontology must pass
topics.what_it_is: A competency question is a question that the finished ontology, with its knowledge base, must be able to answer. Grüninger and Fox (1995) proposed to use such questions to specify and evaluate an ontology. Noy and McGuinness (2001) call them the litmus test: does the ontology contain enough information to answer them? The questions are a sketch, not an exhaustive list. Ren et al. (2014) and Wiśniewski et al. (2019) study how to author and formalise them (for example as SPARQL-OWL queries).
topics.why: A GraphRAG schema should come from the questions users ask. A competency question tells you which entity types and relation labels the extractor must produce, and which can be dropped. Feng et al. (2024) use this idea directly: they generate competency questions from a knowledge base, extract relations from them, and ground KG construction in the resulting ontology.

outputs: A test: each question must be answerable from the final knowledge base

steps: Write the scenarios and the users (Noy and McGuinness step 1: domain and scope).
Sketch questions the knowledge base should answer.
Extract the needed terms and relations from the questions.
Build the ontology.
Check: can each question be answered, for example by a query? If not, extend the ontology.
trade_offs: Questions are a sketch: passing them does not prove the ontology is correct or complete (Noy and McGuinness 2001).
Answerability depends on the data too: a good ontology over an empty graph still fails the test.
Natural-language questions are ambiguous; Wiśniewski et al. (2019) analyse CQ patterns and their formalisation because the step to a query is not trivial.

topics.title: The schema as part of the GraphRAG extraction prompt
topics.what_it_is: In GraphRAG (Edge et al. 2024), an LLM extracts entities and relationships from each text chunk to build the graph index. The extraction prompt takes a list of entity types: "entity type: One of the following types: [{entity types}]". The paper says the prompts can be tailored to a domain by choosing entity types and few-shot examples. The default prompt extracts broad named entities such as people, places and organizations. So the schema enters GraphRAG as a prompt variable, not as an OWL file.
topics.why: This is the lowest-cost way to use an ontology in GraphRAG: pass its class names into the extraction prompt. It sets which nodes exist and how they are typed. Retrieval and summaries then depend on those types.

inputs: List of entity types (from an ontology)

steps: Pick entity types from the domain ontology or the use case.
Insert them in the extraction prompt, with the allowed relation labels if you have them.
Add domain few-shot examples.
Extract per chunk; build the graph.
Check conformance (see the SHACL topic) and revise the type list.
trade_offs: The type list is only a hint to the model: the real run still produced labels outside the list.
Types chosen for one domain give poor coverage in another (Edge et al. 2024 recommend domain-tailored examples).
Long type lists cost tokens on every chunk call.

topics.title: Ontology learning from text
topics.what_it_is: Ontology learning builds an ontology from text, with little or no manual work. Its tasks climb from terms to concepts, then to a class hierarchy, then to other relations. LLMs4OL (2023) tests LLMs on three of these tasks: term typing, taxonomy discovery and extraction of non-taxonomic relations. It evaluates nine LLM families in a zero-shot setting. Population is the matching step that fills the ontology with instances from text.
topics.why: Most GraphRAG indexers do ontology learning without calling it that. The extractor types entities (term typing), links some of them with is-a (taxonomy discovery) and adds other relations. Seeing these as separate tasks tells you what to measure and what to review.

inputs: Optional seed ontology or type list

steps: Extract candidate terms from the corpus.
Group synonyms and assign each term a type (term typing).
Find is-a links between types or terms (taxonomy discovery).
Find other relations between them (non-taxonomic relation extraction).
Review with a human, then populate the ontology with instances.
trade_offs: LLMs4OL is a zero-shot evaluation on a few knowledge sources (WordNet and others named in its abstract); results do not transfer to every domain without checking.
Automatic hierarchies often mix is-a with part-of: review before using them for reasoning.
Human review is still needed; Shimizu and Hitzler (2024) argue LLM-based ontology engineering needs modular ontologies and human oversight.

worked_example.description: The three ontology-learning tasks, counted on the real extracted graph (138 LLM calls, one per passage). Term typing: 662 terms typed into 9 types. Taxonomy discovery: 87 subclass edges (46 is_a, 41 special_case_of). Non-taxonomic relations: the other 675 edges; 117 of them carry the vague label related_to (17.3%).
worked_example.note: The mapping of edge labels to the three tasks is ours.

topics.title: Ontology reasoning for multi-hop questions
topics.what_it_is: A reasoner adds facts that follow from the ontology. For subclass links, the RDFS rule is transitivity. If x is a subclass of y and y is a subclass of z, then x is a subclass of z. Multi-hop retrieval can use these added links to jump several steps at once. LLM methods such as Think-on-Graph (2023) and Reasoning on Graphs (2023) instead let the LLM explore relations on a knowledge graph step by step. OntGQA (2026) adds type constraints from an ontology to such multi-hop reasoning.
topics.why: Multi-hop questions need paths: first find the method, then its inventor. Entailed links shorten paths and make them explainable. Type constraints stop the path from wandering to the wrong kind of node.

inputs: Graph with typed nodes and subclass edges
Reasoning rules (RDFS or OWL 2 RL) or an LLM that plans the path
outputs: Candidate reasoning paths with the passages behind each edge

steps: Decide which relations are subclass-like (is_a, special_case_of).
Compute the transitive closure of those edges.
Treat the added edges as inferred, with the supporting edges as the explanation.
Search paths of length k that mix inferred and stated edges.
Pass the passages along the path to the LLM.
trade_offs: Rules amplify errors: one wrong is_a edge creates every inferred link above it.
A reasoner needs formal axioms; extracted graphs usually have none, so only simple rules like transitivity are safe.
Open-world reasoning (OWL) does not treat a missing edge as false; a property graph query does. Mixing the two causes surprises.

worked_example.description: Real: the extracted graph has 87 explicit subclass edges (is_a plus special_case_of). The transitive closure has 108 pairs, so rdfs11 adds 21 inferred links. Longest chain: ridge regression -> elastic net -> linear support vector machine (both edges stated by the model; the link ridge regression -> linear SVM is inferred). Bridge question q10 (who popularised the method that selects at most n variables): hop 1 reaches lasso (passage p015), hop 2 follows lasso introduced_by Robert Tibshirani (passages p005, p006); gold passages are p015 and p006.
worked_example.note: Computed by our own few lines of code, not by an OWL reasoner. The edges come from an LLM and were not checked against a gold graph.

topics.title: Ontology Development 101 and reuse
topics.what_it_is: Noy and McGuinness (2001) give a seven-step guide. The steps are: set domain and scope, consider reuse, list terms, define classes, define properties, define facets, create instances. They say there is no one correct way to model a domain, and that development is iterative. Classes should be close to the nouns of your domain, and relations close to its verbs. Reuse means checking whether an existing ontology can be refined or extended before you start. Reuse is required when your system must interact with applications that already use a given ontology or vocabulary.
topics.why: A GraphRAG pipeline that reuses known type and relation names (for example a CS ontology) can link its graph to other graphs and to catalogues. A schema invented from scratch cannot. The seven steps also give a checklist for turning a prompt-level type list into a reviewed schema.

topics.title: Ontology vs taxonomy, thesaurus, schema and knowledge graph
topics.what_it_is: A controlled vocabulary is a list of terms where every term has an unambiguous, non-redundant definition (ANSI/NISO Z39.19-2005, Sec. 4, p.5). A taxonomy puts controlled-vocabulary terms in a hierarchy or polyhierarchy of broader/narrower links (Z39.19 Sec. 5.4.3, p.18). A thesaurus adds synonyms and other labelled relationships between terms (Z39.19 Sec. 5.4.4, p.18); SKOS is the W3C format for both. A schema fixes the shape of data, such as field names and value types. An ontology is a formal, explicit specification of a shared conceptualisation (Studer et al. 1998, p.25): classes, relations with domain and range, and axioms that a reasoner can use. A knowledge graph is a graph of data about real-world entities (Hogan et al. 2021, Sec. 1); it may use a schema or an ontology as its vocabulary, but need not. These terms overlap, and the literature does not give sharp borders between them.
topics.why: A GraphRAG pipeline needs a list of entity types and relation types. A taxonomy gives only 'is a' links. An ontology adds typed relations and axioms, so the system can expand a query to subclasses and can reject an extracted triple that breaks the rules. The KG stores the facts; the ontology says what the facts may mean.

outputs: a controlled vocabulary at one of five levels: term list, taxonomy, thesaurus, schema, ontology
a knowledge graph that uses that vocabulary

symbols: set of labelled edges, each written (v, l, v')
formulas.name: Directed edge-labelled graph (the data model of a knowledge graph)

steps: List the terms of the domain (controlled vocabulary).
Link terms with broader/narrower to get a taxonomy.
Add synonyms and 'related to' links to get a thesaurus (SKOS does this).
Turn the taxonomy into classes (rdfs:subClassOf), name the relations and give each a domain and range.
Add axioms such as transitivity, disjointness or defined classes (OWL); keep checks OWL cannot state (no cycle) in code or SHACL.
Attach instance data with evidence on every edge; the result is a knowledge graph.
trade_offs: Each step up the ladder costs more modelling work and needs more skill.
The word 'ontology' is used for anything from a term list to a full logic theory. State which level you mean.
A taxonomy built with skos:broader does not give instances their superclass types. rdfs:subClassOf does (see worked example).
Hogan et al. call the definition of 'knowledge graph' contentious; do not cite one definition as the standard.

topics.title: OntoRAG-style pipelines: derive the ontology from the corpus, then retrieve with it
topics.what_it_is: OntoRAG (2025) is a pipeline that derives an ontology from unstructured documents and uses it for question answering. The steps are web scraping, PDF parsing, hybrid chunking, information extraction, knowledge-graph construction and ontology creation. It applies the Leiden algorithm to the graph, and each community becomes a candidate ontology class. On one corpus of electrical-relay documents, the authors report comprehensiveness win rates of 85% against vector RAG and 75% against the best GraphRAG configuration.
topics.why: GraphRAG already builds communities with Leiden. OntoRAG reads those communities as ontology classes, so the community structure doubles as a schema that can guide retrieval. The evidence is thin: one preprint, one domain, 4 citations.

outputs: An ontology (classes, relations) derived from graph communities
Answers to sensemaking questions that use the ontology

steps: Parse and chunk the documents.
Extract entities and relations with an LLM.
Build the graph.
Detect communities with Leiden; treat each community as a candidate class.
Name and relate the classes; use them at query time to pick relevant parts of the graph.
trade_offs: Evidence is one domain and an arXiv preprint (single study, 4 citations); treat the win rates as indicative, not general.
Graph communities group related terms; they are not guaranteed to be classes in the is-a sense.
Derived ontologies have no axioms unless extra work is done, so reasoning is limited.

topics.title: Open-world vs closed-world assumption (and unique names)
topics.what_it_is: Under the closed-world assumption (CWA), a fact that is not in the data is false. Under the open-world assumption (OWA), a missing fact is unknown: it may be true somewhere else. OWL and description logics use the open-world assumption and do not assume unique names. Many classical database systems adopt the closed-world assumption (Hogan 2021); a SPARQL query with FILTER NOT EXISTS also acts closed-world on the data it sees. SHACL validates a data graph against shapes in a closed-world style: a missing required value is a violation. The difference explains why an OWL ontology does not 'reject' incomplete data but a SHACL shape does.
topics.why: LLM-extracted graphs are always incomplete. Under OWA the graph never says a fact is false just because it is missing, which is safe for reasoning. For quality control you want the opposite: a lecture with no topic is an error. So use OWL for inference and SHACL for checks.

G
ot\models e\iff G\models
eg e\ (	ext{CWA});\qquad G
ot\models e\ 
ot\Rightarrow\ G\models
eg e\ (	ext{OWA})
formulas.name: Closed-world and open-world reading of absence (Hogan et al. 2021)

steps: Ask: do I want to infer, or to check?
To infer from incomplete data use OWL (open world).
To check completeness use SHACL or a closed query (FILTER NOT EXISTS).
If cardinality is declared in OWL, remember that without unique names a second value merges individuals (owl:sameAs) instead of failing.
Document which layer enforces what.
trade_offs: A maxCardinality axiom in OWL does not signal an error when two different names appear; it infers they are the same individual (no unique name assumption).
An OWL 'minimum one' (someValuesFrom) axiom is never violated by missing data; the reasoner just assumes an unknown value exists.
Mixing OWA ontology and CWA query surprises users: 'no covers triple' in a query does not mean the lecture covers nothing.
Reiter's CWA is not the same as negation as failure in all systems; variations exist (Hogan 2021, footnote).

topics.title: Operational ontology (Palantir style): objects, links and actions
topics.what_it_is: In Palantir Foundry, the Ontology is described as an operational layer for the organization. It sits on top of datasets and models and connects them to real-world counterparts such as plants, products, orders and transactions. It has semantic elements (objects, properties, links) and kinetic elements (actions, functions, dynamic security). An action type defines a set of changes to objects, property values and links. A user makes these changes at once, with side effects such as notifications. The documentation calls it a digital twin of the organization in many settings.

Build applications on top; user decisions return as edits to the Ontology.

topics.title: OWL 2 and description logic (SROIQ)
topics.what_it_is: OWL 2 is the W3C language for ontologies: classes, properties, individuals and axioms. Its formal core is description logic (DL), a decidable fragment of first-order logic. OWL 2 DL corresponds roughly to the description logic SROIQ. Meaning is model-theoretic: an interpretation maps individuals to elements, classes to sets and properties to pairs. A reasoner can derive facts that the author did not write. The full DL has high worst-case cost, so OWL 2 also defines smaller profiles (EL, QL, RL).
topics.why: OWL axioms such as disjointness, equivalence and existential restrictions give a GraphRAG system a precise, checkable schema. They make the multi-hop step explainable: each inferred edge has a proof. They also cost expertise and compute, so many GraphRAG stacks use only a small subset.

inputs: an OWL 2 ontology (axioms) and optionally instance data

formulas.latex: \mathcal I=(\Delta^{\mathcal I},\cdot^{\mathcal I}),\ a^{\mathcal I}\in\Delta^{\mathcal I},\ C^{\mathcal I}\subseteq\Delta^{\mathcal I},\ R^{\mathcal I}\subseteq\Delta^{\mathcal I}\times\Delta^{\mathcal I};\quad (\exists R.C)^{\mathcal I}=\{a\mid\exists b:(a,b)\in R^{\mathcal I}\wedge b\in C^{\mathcal I}\};\quad (\forall R.C)^{\mathcal I}=\{a\mid\forall b:(a,b)\in R^{\mathcal I}\Rightarrow b\in C^{\mathcal I}\};\quad \mathcal I\models C\sqsubseteq D\iff C^{\mathcal I}\subseteq D^{\mathcal I}
symbols: domain of the interpretation (set of individuals)
formulas.name: DL interpretation and semantics of main constructors

formulas.latex: \mathcal K=(\mathcal A,\mathcal T,\mathcal R);\qquad \mathcal K_1\models\mathcal K_2\iff \text{every model of }\mathcal K_1\text{ is a model of }\mathcal K_2
formulas.name: Knowledge base and entailment

steps: Model classes, properties and individuals.
Add axioms (subclass, equivalence, disjointness, restrictions, property characteristics).
Run a reasoner: check consistency, then classify.
Inspect inferred subsumptions and unsatisfiable classes.
Fix the axioms that caused surprises.
trade_offs: Unrestricted use of all DL constructors makes entailment undecidable (Hogan 2021, Appendix B.5.3); OWL 2 DL restricts them.
OWL 2 DL (Direct Semantics) reasoning is N2EXPTIME-complete in combined complexity (W3C Profiles Table 10).
OWL has the open-world assumption and no unique name assumption: missing data is unknown, not false.
OWL 2 Full (RDF-Based Semantics) is undecidable (same table). Use OWL 2 DL or a profile for tools.
Not every graph is a well-formed OWL 2 DL ontology; Hogan 2021 gives the sub-taxon-of example that cannot be written in DL.

topics.title: OWL 2 profiles: EL, QL and RL
topics.what_it_is: An OWL 2 profile is a trimmed-down version of OWL 2 that trades expressive power for efficient reasoning. OWL 2 EL allows existential restrictions and intersections but no universal restrictions, union or negation; it suits very large class hierarchies such as SNOMED CT. OWL 2 QL restricts where constructs may appear so that queries can be rewritten into relational queries; it suits big instance data. OWL 2 RL restricts constructs to syntactic positions so a rule engine can do the reasoning; it suits rule-based triple stores. The three profiles are independent; none contains the others. Pick the profile from the shape of your ontology and the reasoning task.
topics.why: A production GraphRAG graph can hold millions of nodes. Full OWL 2 DL reasoning does not scale to that. A profile gives a guarantee: EL for a huge schema, QL for query answering over a big database, RL for materialising inferences with rules in a triple store.

inputs: the reasoning task (classification, query answering, materialisation)
outputs: the complexity guarantee that profile gives

formulas.latex: \begin{array}{lll}\text{OWL 2 DL: } & \text{N2EXPTIME-complete} & \text{(combined)}\\ \text{OWL 2 EL: } & \text{PTIME-complete} & \text{(consistency, subsumption, instance checking)}\\ \text{OWL 2 QL: } & \text{NLogSpace-complete; data complexity in AC}^0 & \text{(consistency, subsumption, instance checking)}\\ \text{OWL 2 RL: } & \text{PTIME-complete} & \text{(consistency, subsumption, instance checking)}\end{array}
symbols: very low parallel complexity class; query answering over data can be done like in a relational database
formulas.name: Complexity guarantees (W3C Profiles, Table 10, Direct Semantics)

steps: List the constructs your ontology uses.
Check each class expression against the profile tables (EL: Section 2.2; QL: Table 1; RL: Table 2).
If one profile fits, use a reasoner built for it (ELK for EL, a rewriter such as Ontop for QL, a rule engine for RL).
If none fits, use an OWL 2 DL reasoner (HermiT, Pellet) and accept the cost.
Keep the profile as a design rule: lint new axioms against it.
trade_offs: Moving a single axiom out of a profile (for example one union in a superclass position) removes the guarantee.
An RL rule engine can miss entailments that a DL reasoner finds when the ontology is outside RL (see worked example).
QL cannot express transitive properties or property chains (property inclusion 'not involving property chains').
EL has no negation and no universal restriction, so it cannot state 'every course covers only topics from this list'.

topics.title: Property graph vs RDF
topics.what_it_is: In RDF a graph is a set of subject-predicate-object triples with global IRIs. In a property graph every node and every edge can carry a label and key-value properties. Neo4j is the best-known property graph database; its query language is Cypher. Property graphs can be translated to and from directed edge-labelled graphs such as RDF without loss of information. RDF has standards for schema, reasoning and exchange (RDFS, OWL, SHACL, SPARQL); property graphs have a flexible edge model and fast traversal. RDF 1.2 and RDF-star add triple terms so that a statement can carry its own properties.
topics.why: Most GraphRAG tools store a property graph (Neo4j); most ontology tools speak RDF. You need a bridge. The data models are inter-translatable, but the semantics layer (class hierarchy, constraints, reasoning) is richer in RDF, so decide which layer owns the schema.

outputs: the same information in the other model

maps a node or edge to a set of labels

steps: Decide the system of record: RDF store or property graph.
Map entity IRIs to node ids and relation IRIs to edge types.
Decide how to keep edge properties: reification, named graph, RDF-star/RDF 1.2 triple term, or an intermediate node.
Keep schema in one place (SHACL for RDF; constraints and labels for Neo4j) and generate the other.
Test round-trip (graph to RDF and back) on a sample.
trade_offs: Plain RDF 1.1 cannot put a property on one edge; the common workaround (reification) needs 4 extra triples per statement.
Property graph labels are not IRIs, so cross-database meaning needs a mapping such as n10s namespaces.
Neo4j does not do OWL reasoning; 'inference' there is label and hierarchy traversal (see neo4j-n10s).
The choice is often 'secondary to practical factors such as available implementations' (Hogan et al. 2021, Section 2.1.3).

topics.title: RDF datasets, named graphs and serialisations (Turtle, N-Triples, TriG, JSON-LD)
topics.what_it_is: An RDF dataset holds one default graph and zero or more named graphs; each named graph has an IRI or blank node as its name. A named graph lets you attach facts about a set of triples, such as the source, date or trust level. A serialisation is a text format for an RDF graph or dataset. Turtle is the compact human format; N-Triples is one triple per line; TriG and N-Quads add graph names; JSON-LD uses JSON. Different serialisations of the same graph have the same meaning. The RDF 1.1 dataset specification gives no single agreed formal meaning for a named graph's name.
topics.why: In GraphRAG each extracted triple should keep its source passage and run id. Named graphs are the standard way to do this in RDF: one graph per document or per extraction run. Retrieval can then filter by source or trust.

inputs: triples plus a graph name per group of triples
outputs: files in TriG, N-Quads, Turtle, N-Triples or JSON-LD

steps: Group triples by source or run.
Give each group an IRI as its graph name.
Write the metadata about the group in the default graph or in a meta graph.
Save as TriG or N-Quads; load into a triple store that supports datasets.
Query with SPARQL GRAPH ?g { ... } to filter by source.
trade_offs: Graph names are not part of the RDF 1.1 semantics: the spec leaves the meaning of a graph name open.
A graph name is just a label for a set of triples; it does not make the triples true or false.
Named graphs are coarse. Statements about a single triple need reification, RDF-star or RDF 1.2 triple terms (see property-graph-vs-rdf).
Turtle and N-Triples cannot carry graph names; use TriG or N-Quads.

topics.title: RDF: triples, IRIs, literals and blank nodes
topics.what_it_is: RDF is the W3C data model that writes every fact as a triple: subject, predicate, object. A subject is an IRI or a blank node; a predicate is an IRI; an object is an IRI, a literal or a blank node. An IRI is a global name for a thing, such as http://example.org/CNN4. A literal is a value with a datatype or a language tag, such as "90"^^xsd:integer or "Netz"@de. A blank node is a local node without a global name; its identifier has meaning only inside one file or store. A set of triples is an RDF graph; the nodes are the subjects and objects.
topics.why: GraphRAG systems that emit RDF get global entity names (IRIs), typed values (literals) and a standard exchange format. Entity linking maps a text mention to an IRI, so two documents can point to the same node. Blank nodes are a trap: they cannot be linked across files.

outputs: serialisations such as Turtle, N-Triples, JSON-LD

symbols: set of blank nodes (disjoint from I and L)
RDF graph: a finite set of triples

steps: Choose an IRI for each entity and each relation.
Write facts as triples; use a literal for a plain value.
Use a blank node only for a thing that needs no global name.
Serialise (Turtle for people, N-Triples for tools, JSON-LD for web APIs).
Load the graph into a triple store or into a library such as rdflib.
trade_offs: Blank node identifiers are local to a file: the same _:b1 in two files is not the same node.
An IRI and a string with the same characters are different terms; "http://example.org/" is not http://example.org/.
A predicate IRI may also appear as a node in the same graph (allowed by the spec).
RDF 1.2 (Candidate Recommendation, 2026-04-07) adds triple terms and directional language-tagged strings; RDF 1.1 is the current Recommendation.

topics.title: RDFS: classes, subclass, subproperty, domain and range
topics.what_it_is: RDF Schema (RDFS) is a small vocabulary on top of RDF for describing classes and properties. rdfs:subClassOf says every instance of one class is an instance of another. rdfs:subPropertyOf says every pair linked by one property is also linked by another. rdfs:domain and rdfs:range say which class the subject or the object of a property belongs to. RDFS axioms are used to infer new triples, not to forbid data; a wrong domain just yields a new type. RDFS is the lightweight base that OWL extends.
topics.why: Subclass links let a retriever answer 'neural network' questions with CNN or Transformer nodes. Domain and range give an extracted triple a type check by inference: an odd subject gets a surprising type, which is a warning sign. They are the cheapest ontology features to add.

Query the closure.
trade_offs: Domain and range are inference rules, not constraints. Use SHACL to reject bad data.
Two domains on one property are intersected, not alternatives; a common modelling error.
RDFS has no negation, no disjointness and no cardinality; use OWL for these.
A materialised closure can be large; store it or compute it at query time.

topics.title: Reasoning tasks and reasoners (subsumption, consistency, instance checking; HermiT, Pellet, ELK)
topics.what_it_is: A reasoner is a program that derives the logical consequences of an ontology. Consistency checking asks whether the ontology has any model at all. Subsumption (classification) asks whether one class is always a subclass of another, and builds the class hierarchy. Instance checking asks whether an individual belongs to a class; it can also be used to realise, i.e. find the most specific classes. HermiT and Pellet are complete OWL 2 DL reasoners; ELK is a fast reasoner for the OWL 2 EL profile. Many standard reasoning problems can be reduced to each other, so one algorithm handles them all.
topics.why: Reasoning turns a stored graph into a bigger, explained graph: new type edges, a class hierarchy for query expansion, and a consistency alarm when an extracted triple contradicts the schema. It can be run offline and the result materialised, so the retriever stays fast.

inputs: a task: consistency, classification, instance checking

formulas.latex: \text{consistency: }\exists\,\mathcal I:\ \mathcal I\models\mathcal K;\qquad \text{subsumption: }\mathcal K\models C\sqsubseteq D\iff\forall\mathcal I\models\mathcal K:\ C^{\mathcal I}\subseteq D^{\mathcal I};\qquad \text{instance checking: }\mathcal K\models C(a)\iff\forall\mathcal I\models\mathcal K:\ a^{\mathcal I}\in C^{\mathcal I}
symbols: I is a model of K
formulas.name: The three standard reasoning tasks

steps: Load the ontology into the reasoner.
Check consistency first; an inconsistent ontology entails everything.
Classify: compute the subsumption hierarchy and look for unsatisfiable classes.
Realise: compute the inferred types of individuals.
Export or materialise the inferred axioms for the query layer.
trade_offs: An inconsistent ontology makes every axiom hold vacuously (Krotzsch et al. 2012), so check it before trusting any answer.
Full OWL 2 DL reasoning is N2EXPTIME-complete in the worst case; real ontologies are usually much easier, but not always.
Use ELK only on EL ontologies; it ignores or rejects constructs outside EL (check its documentation before relying on it; not tested here).
Reasoners differ in coverage and speed. Results should agree on OWL 2 DL; test two reasoners when it matters.

topics.title: SHACL: validating graphs against shapes
topics.what_it_is: SHACL (Shapes Constraint Language) is a W3C language to validate an RDF data graph against a shapes graph. A node shape says which nodes are targeted, for example all instances of a class. A property shape puts constraints on one path, such as sh:minCount, sh:datatype or sh:class. The validator returns a validation report with a result for each violation. SHACL checks the data as given; it does not infer new facts, and it treats missing values as errors where a shape requires them. SHACL Core is a Recommendation (2017); SHACL 1.2 is a Working Draft.
topics.why: An LLM extracts triples that may be wrong or incomplete. SHACL is the gate: it rejects a triple whose object has the wrong type, a value with the wrong datatype, or an entity that lacks a required property. It turns the ontology's intent into a pass/fail check before the triple enters the graph.

outputs: validation report: conforms true/false, and a result per violation (focus node, path, constraint component, message)

formulas.latex: [\xrightarrow{p}\varphi\{min,max\}]^{G,v,\sigma}=1\iff min\le\bigl|\{(v,p,u)\in E\mid[\varphi]^{G,u,\sigma}=1\}\bigr|\le max;\qquad G\text{ valid under }(\Sigma,T)\iff\exists\sigma:\ \sigma(v,s)=[\lambda(s)]^{G,v,\sigma}\ \wedge\ ((v,s)\in T\Rightarrow\sigma(v,s)=1)
symbols: shapes map: which node satisfies which shape label
shapes target: pairs (node, shape label) that must hold
formulas.name: Shape evaluation (cardinality constraint) and valid graph

steps: Write a node shape with sh:targetClass.
Add property shapes: path, sh:minCount, sh:maxCount, sh:datatype, sh:class, sh:pattern.
Run a validator (pySHACL, Jena SHACL, TopBraid, n10s).
Read the report; fix data or relax shapes.
Gate extraction: only accept triples that pass.
trade_offs: SHACL does not do OWL reasoning unless you ask the validator for RDFS/OWL-RL inference first; results can then differ.
Cardinality in SHACL counts triples present in the data; in OWL it does not (open world).
One sh:message on a property shape is reused for all constraint components of that shape (see report below), so write distinct shapes for distinct messages.
SHACL-SPARQL and rules (SHACL Advanced Features) are separate from Core; the rules document is only a W3C Working Group Note.
SHACL 1.2 Core is a Working Draft: do not cite it as final.

topics.title: SKOS: thesauri and concept schemes on the web
topics.what_it_is: SKOS (Simple Knowledge Organization System) is a W3C vocabulary for thesauri, taxonomies and classification schemes. A skos:Concept is an idea; a skos:ConceptScheme groups concepts. skos:prefLabel and skos:altLabel give the preferred name and synonyms, in several languages. skos:broader, skos:narrower and skos:related link concepts; skos:broaderTransitive covers the whole chain. skos:broader is not rdfs:subClassOf: it links concepts without saying that instances inherit. SKOS works well to publish and map existing vocabularies; it is lighter than OWL.
topics.why: Many real vocabularies (subject headings, course topics, ACM CCS, MeSH) are SKOS. A GraphRAG pipeline can use altLabels for entity linking and broader/narrower links for query expansion, without a full ontology. It is the cheapest source of synonyms.

inputs: a list of concepts with labels and broader/narrower links
outputs: a SKOS concept scheme in RDF
synonym lists and hierarchy for lookup

steps: Declare a skos:ConceptScheme.
Give each concept a prefLabel (one per language) and optional altLabels.
Link with skos:broader and skos:narrower; mark top concepts.
Add skos:exactMatch or closeMatch to concepts in other schemes.
Publish as RDF and index the labels.
trade_offs: SKOS broader is not 'is a': a concept can be broader for part-of or topic reasons. Do not infer instance types from it.
The SKOS spec defines its data model as an OWL Full ontology and states that fewer integrity conditions apply than in a closed-world database.
skos:broader is not declared transitive; use skos:broaderTransitive or a property path.
Mixing SKOS and OWL on the same resource (punning) needs care.

worked_example.description: A three-level concept scheme. SPARQL property path skos:broader+ finds the ancestors of Deep learning. An RDFS closure adds types but does not add ':DL a :AI'.

:ML a skos:Concept ; skos:prefLabel "Machine learning"@en ; skos:altLabel "ML"@en ; skos:broader :AI .
:DL a skos:Concept ; skos:prefLabel "Deep learning"@en ; skos:broader :ML .
:cs a skos:ConceptScheme .

topics.title: SPARQL: querying RDF graphs
topics.what_it_is: SPARQL is the W3C query language for RDF. A query holds triple patterns with variables; the engine returns every way to bind the variables so the pattern matches the graph. Query forms are SELECT (a table), ASK (yes or no), CONSTRUCT and DESCRIBE (new RDF). Property paths such as rdfs:subClassOf* follow chains of edges, which gives subclass-aware queries without a reasoner. The GRAPH keyword matches patterns inside named graphs of a dataset. SPARQL 1.1 also has UPDATE, federation (SERVICE), aggregates and NOT EXISTS.
topics.why: SPARQL is the retrieval language of an RDF knowledge graph. A GraphRAG system can turn a question into a SPARQL query, or run fixed queries: type filters, subclass expansion with a property path, and provenance filters with GRAPH. The result rows become the context for the LLM.

outputs: SELECT: a table of variable bindings

symbols: solution mapping: partial function from variables V to RDF terms T
compatible: they agree on shared variables
formulas.name: Solution mappings and join (SPARQL 1.1 algebra)

steps: Write triple patterns with ?variables.
Combine them in a basic graph pattern (a join).
Add OPTIONAL, FILTER, UNION, FILTER NOT EXISTS as needed.
Use property paths (a/rdfs:subClassOf*) for hierarchies.
Choose SELECT, ASK or CONSTRUCT and run against a store or a library.
trade_offs: SPARQL matches the stored triples; without a reasoner it does not know subclass facts unless you use a property path or materialise them.
FILTER NOT EXISTS is closed-world over the stored data (see open-vs-closed-world).
Unbounded property paths on large graphs can be slow.
LLM-generated SPARQL can be wrong; validate by running ASK or by checking vocabulary terms against the ontology.

worked_example.description: Models in a graph; find everything that is a kind of NeuralNetwork (using a property path) and optionally its training dataset. Counts of instances.
worked_example.code:
PREFIX : <http://example.org/>
PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
SELECT ?m ?d WHERE { ?m a/rdfs:subClassOf* :NeuralNetwork . OPTIONAL { ?m :trainedOn ?d } } ORDER BY ?m
# data: CNN, Transformer are subclasses of NeuralNetwork; alexnet and resnet are CNN; bert is a Transformer; alexnet :trainedOn :ImageNet
worked_example.result: SELECT returns 3 rows: (alexnet, ImageNet), (bert, none), (resnet, none). 'ASK { :bert a :NeuralNetwork }' returns false, because the triple is not stored (no reasoning). 'SELECT (COUNT(?m)) WHERE { ?m a :CNN }' returns 2.

topics.title: T-Box, A-Box and R-Box
topics.what_it_is: A description-logic knowledge base is split into three sets of axioms: the A-Box, the T-Box and the R-Box. The A-Box holds assertions about named individuals: class assertions and property assertions. The T-Box holds class (terminological) axioms, such as Mother is a subclass of Parent. The R-Box holds role (property) axioms, such as parentOf is a subproperty of ancestorOf, or transitivity. From the logic side the split is customary only; there is no principal difference between the axiom types. OWL 2 itself speaks of axioms and assertions and does not use the words T-Box or A-Box.
topics.why: The split tells you what to freeze and what to grow. The T-Box and R-Box are the schema: small, reviewed, versioned. The A-Box is the knowledge graph that GraphRAG extracts from text and grows all the time. Validation and update rules differ for the two parts.

inputs: an ontology file with mixed axioms
outputs: three groups: terminology (T), role axioms (R), assertions (A)

formulas.latex: \mathcal K=(\mathcal A,\mathcal T,\mathcal R)\quad\text{with example}\quad \mathcal A=\{City(Arica),\,flight(Arica,Santiago)\},\ \mathcal T=\{City\sqsubseteq Place\},\ \mathcal R=\{flight\sqsubseteq connectsTo\}
formulas.name: DL knowledge base

steps: Take an ontology in Turtle or RDF/XML.
Put class axioms (subClassOf, equivalentClass, disjointWith, restrictions) in T.
Put property axioms (subPropertyOf, inverseOf, transitive, symmetric) in R; domain and range are class inclusions, so they go in T.
Put class assertions and property assertions on named individuals in A.
Version T and R together; stream A.
trade_offs: Domain and range are written as class inclusions in DL (domain Event for venue becomes: exists venue.Top is a subclass of Event, Hogan 2021 App. B), so they count as T-Box axioms, although OWL 2 syntax lists them with property axioms. Tutorials differ.
The border is blurred in RDF: both parts are triples in one graph, and a class can be an individual (punning).
SHACL shapes are not a T-Box: they are a separate input to a validator with closed-world style checking.
No source read uses 'X-Box' or 'C-Box'.

worked_example.description: Split a tiny RDF graph into T, R and A by predicate. Counting by rule (ours): class axioms (subClassOf, equivalentClass, disjointWith) -> T; property axioms (subPropertyOf, inverseOf, characteristics such as transitive) -> R; domain and range -> T (they are class inclusions in DL); everything else with rdf:type to a non-OWL class or a plain property -> A.
worked_example.code:
@prefix : <http://example.org/> . @prefix owl: <http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#> . @prefix rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#> .
:MLLecture rdfs:subClassOf :Lecture .          # T
:Lecture owl:disjointWith :Person .            # T
:covers rdfs:domain :Lecture ; rdfs:range :Topic .  # T (as class inclusions)
:partOf a owl:TransitiveProperty .             # R
:l1 a :Lecture ; :covers :Backprop .           # A
worked_example.result: By construction: T = 4 axioms (subclass, disjointness, domain, range), R = 1 axiom (transitive partOf), A = 2 assertions. This is an illustration of the split, not output of a tool; the split rule is ours, not from a standard.

topics.title: Type-aware retrieval and subclass expansion
topics.what_it_is: Subclass expansion widens a query with the narrower classes of the query concept. A query about regularization also reaches ridge regression, dropout and early stopping. This is ontology-based query expansion, reviewed by Bhogal, Macfarlane and Smith (2007). Type-aware retrieval filters or ranks graph nodes by their ontology type. OntGQA (2026) uses a relation-centric ontology graph, where each relation carries its head and tail entity types, to constrain multi-hop paths.
topics.why: Entity linking often hits a general node while the answer sits on a narrower node. Expanding along subclass edges gets there. A type filter cuts the neighbours of a hub node to the kind you need.

inputs: Query concept linked to a node
Subclass edges (is_a, special_case_of) and node types
outputs: An expanded set of nodes and their source passages

steps: Link the query to a node.
Collect all nodes below it along subclass edges (one level or the transitive closure).
Optionally keep only nodes of the wanted type.
Gather the passages of these nodes.
Rank and give them to the LLM.
trade_offs: Expansion adds noise: broad classes pull in many passages (regularization: from 10 to 19).
Extracted subclass edges can be wrong; 29 of 87 cross entity types in the real graph.
Classical query-expansion studies report mixed gains; the review by Bhogal et al. covers the trade-offs (title and venue verified, text not read).

worked_example.description: Real numbers on the extracted graph. The node "regularized regression techniques" is in 1 passage (p074). One level of subclass expansion adds ridge regression, lasso, Elastic Net Regression and spike-and-slab regression, and the passage set grows to 15, including p002, the second gold passage of bridge question q09 (who introduced ridge regression: Hoerl and Kennard, 1970). Another case: "regularization" has 8 direct subclasses, and its passages grow from 10 to 19. Type filter: regularization has 29 edges to neighbours (Method 13, Concept 10, Property 4, Other 2); a Method-only filter keeps 13 (45%).
worked_example.note: Not an evaluation: one question, graph as extracted by an LLM without gold check. The gold-passage check shows reachability, not answer quality.
